author.name: Joseph Conrad
author.occupation: Polish-British novelist and former merchant seaman
author.biography: Born into a Polish family under Russian rule, Conrad spent years at sea before becoming a writer in English, a language he acquired as an adult. Ships and imperial routes gave him close views of how authority behaves far from the people who authorise it. Conrad travelled to the Congo as a merchant seaman in 1890. That experience lies behind Marlow's journey into a system whose civilising claims conceal exploitation and violence.

hook.text: What would happen to your principles if nobody could hold you to them?

paragraphs: Marlow takes a job that will carry him up an African river to meet a man named Kurtz. Long before they meet, he hears what an exceptional person Kurtz is: gifted, persuasive, capable of extraordinary results.

The journey exposes a widening distance between those descriptions and the world around them. Trade and civilisation provide a respectable vocabulary. Exhaustion, brutality and indifference reveal what that vocabulary can hide. The question becomes what authority does to a person when its usual restraints have disappeared.

Conrad makes us listen through layers of narration. Marlow is recalling an experience he cannot comfortably explain, and his perceptions deserve scrutiny of their own. The African people around him are often denied the individuality his story gives to Europeans. That limitation is part of what later readers have challenged.
Read for what the narrator sees, what he cannot see and what he chooses to protect. How much of a moral identity depends on the presence of people who can answer back?

orientation.text: An unnamed listener frames Marlow's account. Keep the narrator, Marlow and Conrad distinct; the story's perspective is one of its difficulties.
